claim: Learning disabilities in children: general (not frontal-only) theta power increase at rest
detail: Children with learning disabilities and healthy controls (n=216 in total) with eyes-open and eyes-closed resting EEG. Theta power was increased across the scalp, with no matching posterior alpha decrease. Beta power was higher at frontal electrodes in the learning-disabled group; this is not coded because the electrode names are not in the abstract, so only theta is recorded. Coherence changes are connectivity and are not coded. Taken from the abstract; not checked in the full text. Case-control clinical study; group sizes not given in the abstract.

cite.title: Resting-state electroencephalogram in learning-disabled children: power and connectivity analyses.

claim: Developmental dyslexia (Chinese children): lower resting alpha power over all scalp regions
detail: 85 Hong Kong Chinese children with developmental dyslexia and 51 typically developing peers aged 7-11, eyes-closed resting EEG. Alpha power was reduced over central, frontal, temporal, parietal and occipital areas at rest, so sites are coded as whole-head. Network (minimum spanning tree) results and the task recording are not coded. Coded from the full text read in an earlier pass of this batch.

claim: Learning disabilities in children: higher theta/beta and theta/alpha resting ratios than controls
detail: Children with learning disabilities (non-specified and verbal subtypes) compared with healthy controls, resting EEG. Theta/beta and theta/alpha ratios were larger in learning-disabled children, and frontal independent components showed slowing; the verbal and non-specified subtypes differed. The ratios are coded as theta up, beta down and alpha down. Component source locations are not given as electrode sites, so sites are whole-head. Taken from the abstract; not checked in the full text. Group sizes are not given in the abstract.

cite.title: Resting State EEG in Children With Learning Disabilities: An Independent Component Analysis Approach.

claim: Learning disabilities in children: higher delta and theta power; alpha pattern mixed by measure
detail: 36 children with learning disabilities and 36 age-, sex- and maternal-education-matched controls, awake resting EEG. Absolute delta, theta and alpha-1 power and relative theta were higher, and relative alpha-2 was lower, at most electrodes, so sites are whole-head. The alpha direction differs by measure, so it is coded as mixed. Links with IQ are not coded. Taken from the abstract; not checked in the full text.

claim: Dyslexia (children): lower source-level delta and theta power over left parieto-occipital regions
detail: 70 children with dyslexia and 50 typically developing controls, 50 s of awake resting clinical EEG, source-reconstructed. Lower delta and theta power was found in left parieto-occipital regions; the sites are the closest 10-20 labels for that source region (P3, T5, O1). Connectivity results are not coded. No significant correlation with IQ, reading or spelling scores. Taken from the abstract; not checked in the full text. Retrospective clinical data with no blinding.

cite.title: Source reconstruction of clinical resting-state EEG reveals differences in power and functional connectivity in children with developmental dyslexia.

claim: Dyslexic boys: lower beta (19-24 Hz) power at bilateral central, parietal and mid-temporal leads
detail: Dyslexic and control boys aged 9-13, resting eyes-open and eyes-closed EEG, in two cohorts with repeat testing. In dyslexics, 19-24 Hz power was lower at bilateral central, parietal and mid-temporal leads. Delta and theta did not differ, and alpha was inconsistent between cohorts. The abstract's region names are mapped to C3/C4, P3/P4 and T3/T4. Taken from the abstract; not checked in the full text. Group sizes are not given in the abstract.

claim: Dyslexic children: lower eyes-closed alpha-2 and alpha-3 source amplitude over parietal, occipital and temporal regions
detail: 26 dyslexic and 11 control children, eyes-closed resting EEG with LORETA source estimates. Parietal, occipital and temporal alpha-2 and alpha-3 sources had lower amplitude in dyslexics; the sites are mapped from the region names to P3, Pz, P4, O1, O2, T5 and T6. Lower alpha was linked to faster pseudo-word reading in some regions. Taken from the abstract; not checked in the full text. Small case-control study.
